data.content_ref: inline:{"analogy":{"adopted_commitment_refs":[],"disanalogies":["An expert's implicit model may use features that cannot be verbalized or included in a checklist, giving it access to information the panel lacks.","An explicit checklist is fixed and auditable; an expert's implicit model can adapt to contextual cues not in the checklist.","The expert is a single instance; the panel is an ensemble. The comparison confounds decomposition-method with aggregation-method."],"overturn_conditions":["If the expert's implicit model is revealed to use the exact same cues as the checklist, the 'explicit vs. implicit' frame is vacuous and the only variable is aggregation.","If the task is such that an explicit checklist cannot represent the necessary cue-interactions, the expert dominates and the panel is a strict loss."],"shared_structure":["Both expert intuition and explicit checklists are cue-integration systems; the difference is whether the integration function is explicit or implicit.","In both cases, reliability depends on the validity and calibration of the cue-weights, not on the explicitness per se.","An implicit model and an explicit model of the same task can be compared by their predictive error on held-out cases."],"source_memory_refs":["SRC_003","SCR_002"],"transfer_claims":["From model comparison theory: one can compare an implicit (expert) and explicit (panel) model using predictive accuracy on a common test set, but only if both are evaluated on the same cases.","The bias-variance tradeoff transfers: the expert may have low bias but high variance (single judge), while the panel may have higher bias (checklist imperfection) but lower variance (aggregation). The winner depends on the task's error structure.","The concept of 'model capacity' transfers: an expert's implicit model may have higher capacity (more features, non-linear interactions) than a checklist, making it better on complex tasks and worse on simple ones."]},"claim":"The debate is a false dichotomy: expert intuition is itself an implicit checklist, so the comparison is not 'checklist vs. intuition' but 'explicit, aggregable structure vs. implicit, non-aggregable structure.' The panel wins only when the explicit checklist's externalized decomposition cancels more noise than the expert's internal decomposition, which is an empirical question about the psychometric structure of the task, not a general principle favoring panels.","counterconditions":[{"case":"If the expert's internal cue-weighting is shown to be as well-calibrated as the explicit checklist's weights, the panel offers no reliability advantage.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"If the expert can verbalize their internal checklist and it matches the external one, the distinction collapses and the panel's only advantage is aggregation, which is independent of the checklist.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"If the task requires cues that are perceptual or holistic (e.g., chess pattern recognition), an explicit verbal checklist may fail to capture them, and the expert's implicit integration dominates.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"}],"definitions":[],"derivation":[],"formalization_refs":[],"mechanism":"An expert's intuition is a learned, internalized cue-weighting function\u2014effectively an implicit regression on features. A non-expert panel with an explicit checklist is also a cue-weighting function, but one where the weights are externally specified and the inputs are aggregated across independent judges. The question becomes: which decomposition has lower variance? The expert's implicit function is opaque and cannot be audited or averaged across instances; the panel's explicit function can be audited and averaged. If the expert's internal weights are well-calibrated (high internal validity), the panel adds nothing. If they are not, the explicit checklist's error-correction dominates.","premises":[],"schema":"deepreason-reasoning-envelope-v1","scope":{"covers":[],"excludes":[]},"simulation_refs":[],"uncertainties":[]}
